items.question: Why did you design Humanity's Last Exam as a global effort with experts contributing just a few questions each?
items.object: The design of Humanity's Last Exam
items.answer: The MMLU dataset, which I made as a graduate student some years ago, was getting saturated. It seemed that pretty much all of the evaluations were getting saturated, so people didn't really know what was going on with AI capabilities. So there seemed to be particularly strong reasons for people to be informed about developments and to develop something new. I was also experiencing that people—experts—don't really have datasets in them. You can't just hire a few experts and they can come up with a dataset. They don't have enough complicated ideas in them. However, I think individual experts might have a question in them instead. So with Humanity's Last Exam, the idea was we have a global effort, with various postdocs and professors each contributing a question or a few questions to stump existing AI systems. These are questions that they would find very difficult to answer. They would find it impressive if the AI systems could answer them. And this would be approximating the human frontier, in some sense, of knowledge and reasoning for closed-ended questions where we already know the answer. So we did that for some months, and we got several thousand questions out of that.

items.question: What would solving Humanity's Last Exam signify to you about AI capabilities?
items.object: The significance and limits of solving Humanity's Last Exam
items.answer: I think this will be a good tracker for whether AI systems can automate a lot of the theoretical parts of sciences, whether they can solve difficult analytic questions. Not experimental; it doesn't test its ability to run biology experiments. That's more motor skills, among other things, or requires motor skills. But for things that are more mathematically related or require some very complex reasoning, that's what this captures. I think that when it's solved, it's roughly the end of a genre, or near the end of a genre, of asking it closed-ended questions for which there are objective answers. It seems like that would be toward the end of it. I think individual problems that it would solve in the future would be interesting enough to be papers in their own right. So once we get through this set of questions, the types of problems it could tackle would be questions worthy of their own paper, like it solved a conjecture, for instance. So it's tracking the ability level up to the point where individual questions themselves are very interesting instead of just the dataset.

items.question: How do you see Humanity's Last Exam's place in the future of AI evaluation?
items.object: Humanity's Last Exam and the limits of closed-ended AI benchmarks
items.answer: In difficulty, it's tough to think of more challenging data-generating processes than taking global experts and, if the subject or genre is closed-ended questions, asking them what's the hardest closed-ended question and crowdsourcing that. But it certainly can get harder where each individual question is open, like conjectures, for instance. But it's true that for benchmarks generally, this would not be the end of the line for AI development, because the AI systems—you know, this doesn't test their ability to move around. This doesn't test their long-term memory. This doesn't test their ability to make PowerPoints, and so on. I think this is still getting at the closed-ended question genre, but not with objective answers that we already know, which is how nearly all benchmarks have been in machine learning. But then we'll be moving over, I think, as a community, more to agential types of tasks or tasks that are more economically valuable directly.

items.question: Why do you favor benchmark questions that are hard for both humans and AI over questions that are easy for humans but hard for AI?
items.object: Benchmark questions that are hard for humans and hard for AI
items.answer: I think a reason for focusing on questions that are hard for humans and hard for AIs is because the questions that are easy for humans but hard for AIs are difficult to generate many of, and do it diversely, often. If it's a specific capability, if some people get some specific training data for it, then they automatically have the capability. There can be some pockets where it's harder, such as the ARC datasets. But in general, if you were collecting, like, count the number of Rs in “strawberry,” that dataset will not have much staying power. I think focusing on difficult things that only a few humans can do, or not that many humans can do, is generally going to be more robust.

items.question: How do you think Enigma evaluation captures longer-horizon intellectual work?
items.object: Enigma evaluation benchmark
items.answer: Enigma evaluation is a collection of puzzles. Humanity's Last Exam is getting individual questions that are tough, that an individual with a lot of expertise could solve. Enigma evaluation, you can think of it as like MIT Mystery Hunt. MIT Mystery Hunts are things that happen over a weekend, and a group of MIT students try to solve this puzzle. There are many steps to it. In terms of human compute, so to speak, it takes a lot of human compute to solve it, and it takes groups to solve it as well, and there's not a very high solve rate. So this is very multistep and requires group-level intelligence to be able to have a shot at solving it. We just collected some of those, and I think this approximates longer-horizon types of intellectual tasks. I don't think that will be solved this year at all. I would be very surprised if it would be. I think we have some evaluations that can keep us aware and able to differentiate between models for a while.

items.question: How do you think about the dimensions of intelligence when interpreting AI benchmark performance?
items.object: AI intelligence and the dimensions measured by benchmarks
items.answer: I think they can definitely prioritize some axes that aren't the key bottleneck capabilities. For instance, Humanity's Last Exam gets at mathematical ability, but that's quite separate from various other abilities that it has. Of course it's a combination of many different skills, but I think it very much gets quantitative and mathematical ability that is not necessarily a bottleneck for agency at all. In thinking about intelligence, I tend to think about it on like 10 or so dimensions instead of a monolithic definition or one key metric, and I think some of these benchmarks just get different parts of that. Those dimensions would be things like fluid intelligence, like what the ARC stuff does and what Raven's Progressive Matrices does. There's crystallized intelligence or acquired knowledge, which is what MMLU largely gets at. Does it know a lot about different things? Image classification—is it able to name lots of different species and objects—is also a facet of crystallized intelligence. There's reading and writing ability; it's its own, and scaling substantially helped with that. There's its visual processing ability. How well can it count things in images? Can it discern the latent pattern in an image, for instance? Is it able to generate images with precise specifications? Can it cross out the middle of some different segments? Can it determine the angle of different things in an image? Is this an obtuse angle or an acute angle? There's audio processing ability, short-term memory, long-term memory, input processing speed, output processing speed, all these different things. If you lack any of these—if you can't read and write, for instance, you'd be severely limited. If you don't have a long-term memory, you'll be severely limited. You'll be very difficult to employ. I think there are several bottlenecks that these benchmarks don't particularly get at. When it gets to 100%, people ask why we still don't have something extremely economically valuable. That's a consequence of it just measuring a different facet. I think you just have to get all those axes to get something that is human-level or at the level of a typical human on cognitive tasks, and that might be thought of as AGI.

items.question: How do you think about the limits of evaluating AI intelligence as a collection of separate abilities?
items.object: Evaluating AI intelligence as separate dimensions of ability
items.answer: For human intelligence, it's sometimes factorized in this way. This isn't to say that one shouldn't study the combinations of the skills simultaneously. For example, with long-term memory, there'll be different facets of it. Does it remember things visually? Does it remember things that were more academic that it learned some while ago? Are there some motor skills that it forgot? There can be different facets of these, and I think evaluations can get combinations of them. There is a sense in which one could be too reductionist by looking at those axes, but I think some benchmarks don't cover those almost at all, and some are claiming that one or are just heavily covering one of those axes, such as MMLU, which is primarily getting at crystallized intelligence. That's basically the type of stuff that they test for in school, but it's not necessarily going to help it make a PowerPoint or book a flight or work a random job. It's important not to have these benchmarks be a lens that distorts your view of things, or to view things through those benchmarks solely, because it can often leave out a lot of important bottlenecks.

items.question: Why do you deliberately work across AI research, corporate policy, domestic policy, politics, and geopolitics?
items.object: Working across AI research, corporate policy, domestic policy, politics, and geopolitics
items.answer: I'll deliberately try to move into different areas on a continual basis just because that's what's more interesting. I initially did research, and then there was some amount of corporate policy and things like that while advising for xAI. Then there was a focus on domestic legislation and then geopolitics, and I think right now I'm more interested in political movement-related things. I think it's largely just to keep things interesting. Not solely; it's guided by being useful. But I think that there are often niches that people aren't trying to bring clarity to or advance or think about from the perspective of AI being a very big deal. That's a reason for continually operating at the technical, corporate policy, domestic policy, political, and geopolitical levels. I think that is also necessary for having a holistic understanding of things. You can make proclamations, for instance, like giving a speech at the UN saying we need AI that is safe or transparent. Well, what does that mean? How do you implement that? Is this implementable? What's the standard? You need to have a sense of what's legally feasible at the legislative level. What is actually implementable? What's the compatibility with corporate incentives? Is it going to be something they're going to be fighting too much or not? And then is this actually a real phenomenon at the AI level, or is this just some vague word? There are many words thrown around that don't actually track phenomena or are distinct from general capabilities, and then you're not actually pointing to anything real. You're just pointing to a vibe-based word.

items.answer: I used to wake up almost every day around the time of GPT-4 thinking, “Oh my goodness, this AI stuff.” But I don't know. items.question: Why do you favor a measured approach to catastrophic AI risk?
items.object: A measured approach to communicating and reasoning about catastrophic AI risk
items.answer: Here's the probabilities, roughly, for people conditioned on thinking that you're getting AGI by 2030. Here's what people who think that's plausible would think the risks are. Here are your exposures to these tail risks. Here are the most efficient ways of reducing those tail risks, et cetera. If you're emotionally wound up throughout the whole thing, people shut down and get defensive. I don't think that's prudent or effective, as well as allowing your own emotions to get hijacked. You're having to deal with a lot of variables here. There are a lot of really tricky trade-offs. US versus China competition is a direct trade-off to various other safety things that make AIs more controllable now. Measuring the capabilities of AI systems or tracking those can also help speed them up in some ways. It's pretty tricky business. If there are black-and-white emotions brought to the subject matter, as opposed to there being continuity, I don't think you can reason through this.

items.question: Where do you think the greatest value lies in efforts to solve AI alignment?
items.object: Priorities for solving AI alignment
items.answer: I think generally the political problems—the incentives, giving people things to do that are incentive compatible—is where more of the value is at compared to on the technical side. I would guess if there's a way to reliably get them to tell the truth, for instance, or make them reliably honest, that would be very valuable. It would be solved such that it wouldn't have a severe trade-off, like it wouldn't be much more expensive to run or tank its performance in other axes, like its crystallized knowledge. I think it would be very valuable having it not overtly lie, because then you could build standards around that as well. I think people would reasonably make demands that AI has not lied to them.

items.question: Why are you comfortable describing an AI model's falsehoods under prompting pressure as lying?
items.object: Describing AI falsehoods under prompting pressure as lying
items.answer: We could take, for instance, the MASK benchmark, which tries to measure this. I think if you ask an AI, “Is Paris in Europe?” they have the belief that Paris is in Europe. When they're telling you that Paris is in Antarctica, I think that they are asserting something that they don't hold to be true in almost any other situation. Given that they have so much common sense now and so much world knowledge, if they are saying something in substantial contradiction with it based on or due to some prompting pressure, that suggests that they're caving to a lie. You could say that it's not a lie in some complicated sense because they don't truly understand things, but I think it's behaviorally similar enough that if somebody's applying pressure for it to say falsehoods to other people, it's related to lying enough that I'm comfortable using the label. Is it really a belief? Whatever. I don't know. That's between you and your dictionary.

items.question: What do you mean when you describe an AI capability as emerging?
items.object: Emerging AI capabilities
items.answer: For capabilities to emerge, we see it all the time where you let the model train for some months, harvest it later, and then see what it's capable of. If there's a new qualitatively distinct property that crosses some threshold such that people are noticing it now—maybe it existed in some very weak, faint form before, but it was really unnoticed—I think that's crossed some sort of threshold of visibility and capability. I'd call that an emerging capability. It still could exist in some very weak form beforehand, just as automatic speech recognition capabilities crossed a threshold at one point where people started wanting to use them, whereas earlier nobody would ask the model to transcribe because it would be too unreliable. It crossed some threshold, and now it actually has this qualitatively important capability, whereas it was pretty broken beforehand. That's the sense in which I'm talking about emerging capabilities.

items.question: How do you assess the danger of self-preservation tendencies emerging as AI models scale?

items.question: How do you assess the Manhattan Project-style strategy in Leopold Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness for developing superintelligence before China?
items.object: The Manhattan Project-style strategy for American superintelligence proposed in Leopold Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness
items.answer: Historically, there was *Situational Awareness* by Leopold Aschenbrenner, which was arguing for something like a Manhattan Project for developing AGI and superintelligence before China. So it's basically, let's beat China to the punch, get superintelligence, prevent them from building it, and then the West will dominate the world—a strategy. You could say a take-over-the-world strategy, something like that. I think that has some issues. In particular, it just doesn't think through the game theory or some of the second-order consequences. If the US does the Manhattan Project—let's say Trump gets AGI-pilled and we set a new project up in the desert; we're going to go to Nevada or New Mexico or wherever, build a trillion-dollar data center there, bring some of the top talent from all these labs, and pay them—I just think this has many issues. One is this would be extremely escalatory. China wouldn't just be like, “Oh, they're going to build superintelligence. As written, they're going to use it to have superintelligence, prevent us from having superintelligence, have a monopoly on intelligence and these sorts of capabilities, and they could weaponize it against us.” They would feel extremely threatened by that, by a very concerted effort, if it's trying to do that in a short amount of time or if it's more plausibly on the horizon. This would cause them to do a similar type of project. Would this actually work? Well, you have information-leakage issues. If you're wanting to do that, you're going to need to convince those AI developers to go out and do their last years of labor in the middle of nowhere. It would need to just be Five Eyes countries' people, or people who can get security clearances. It would need to be people who are not easily extortable, for instance. If they're Chinese nationals, they're probably more extortable because they often have family at home. So what are you doing with that talent? A lot of them want to be in the room where it happened. They don't want to be left out. They'll probably go back home to China, and then they'll work on the competing project there. They're a substantial portion of the talent base. I think you're shooting yourself in the foot if you're saying it's only people born and raised in the US who can work on this project, and they're all going to work in unpleasant conditions. This wouldn't be secret. There's almost no way this would be secret. China would very likely know. Such projects would be sabotageable as well. If you're saying, “We'll have it just be an industry or something like that,” then you're not going to have good information security. You're going to have insider-threat issues if people are extortable, and other classic computer-security issues, like they're using Slack. Slack is very easily hackable. They're using iPhones. iPhones are very easily hackable. So you can know what's going on there. You're not actually having much in the way of secrets. Secrecy was very much an advantage for the Manhattan Project, as well as having much more of the talent that can't go to other countries as easily. I just don't think you have that. There are ways in which AI is analogous to nuclear and nuclear weapons and chemical weapons and biological weapons and some of these dual-use technologies, but I don't think the Manhattan Project is one of those things that's analogous.

items.question: How do you think the prospect of imminent superintelligence could push countries toward a deterrence and verification regime?
items.object: Deterrence and cooperation around imminent superintelligence
items.answer: I think the prospect of a superintelligence being imminent is extremely frightening to different actors. If it's imminent, if they have it either way, or if it's being developed and it's arriving in a few months, that's extremely frightening if you miss out on that. What do they want to do? They will either want to prevent such projects or steal it, and so that looks like sabotage, for instance, for prevention. They may have some insider threats who could do some type of sabotage to disrupt this type of project. They could do things like snipe some of the power plants corresponding to the data center. Now your data centers don't work. Was it China? Was it Russia? Was it a US citizen? It's fairly unclear. There are a lot of ways they can have low attributability to prevent this sort of thing from happening. The fact that information—you can't do a secret project really well—is a substantial barrier, and the sabotageability is a substantial barrier, as well as how offensive and nuts you seem if you're saying we're going to build superintelligence and it's going to be explosive. If you're using superintelligence in a thick sense, I think this would be destabilizing. China would reason: if the US controls it, they could weaponize it against us and we get crushed. Or they don't control it because they lose control of it in this process, in which case we also want to prevent it. Either way, we want to prevent it, provided they take this AI stuff seriously. The US would reason the same about China, and Russia, which doesn't have a hope of competing, would definitely want to prevent each other. I think similarly for other nuclear states and other states that have substantial cyber capabilities. This could lead to some type of deterrence dynamic, where they make some attempt at getting superintelligence closer, but then other countries start to express very strong preferences against it. They say, “If you do that, we'll get very mad; there might be a skirmish or something like that.” This may pressure them to move more toward a verification regime, where they aren't trying to make a bid for having some sort of intelligence explosion, having AIs do automated AI research really quickly, like spinning up 100,000 AI instances to do AI research really quickly and bring you from AGI to superintelligence in a short period of time. I think that's a key dynamic: the extent to which it's destabilizing. That strategy needs to keep that in mind. There may be cooperation, but it may be through coercion, by saying we're not going to allow this trajectory or you to make this bid for global dominance. That could give way to something more multilateral and provide some strategic stability.

items.question: How do you adapt nuclear-era strategy into your framework for AI competition?
items.object: The nuclear-era framework and definition of competitiveness in Superintelligence Strategy
items.answer: Overall, the paper talks about three parts. In the nuclear era, we had deterrence through mutual assured destruction. They don't use nukes because we can hit them back. They don't do the superintelligence equivalent. This is kind of like preventing Iran's nuclear program in some way, nobody wanting each other to get the nuclear bomb first or a huge stockpile of nuclear bombs first. In the nuclear context, we also had nonproliferation of fissile materials. We didn't want fissile materials being spread to rogue actors, and we didn't want people having a poor man's atom bomb. That would be very destabilizing and cause lots of catastrophes. We also had containment of the Soviet Union in the geopolitical competition between the two. For AI, we also have a deterrence thing. We also have nonproliferation—in this case, of AI chips to rogue actors like North Korea or Iran or adversaries through export controls. We also have competitiveness with China. Instead of containment of the Soviet Union, this would be competition with China. How do we improve our competitiveness? We want energy for AI data centers. We want secure supply chains so that if Taiwan is invaded, our AI chips aren't cut off. We want secure supply chains for robotics, because if there is a US-China conflict, a lot of that supply chain is currently in China and is very vulnerable. Those are some basic things to improve competitiveness. It's making competitiveness not be “Let's be the first to build superintelligence,” which is what the Manhattan Project strategy pushes toward. Instead, competition is more market share across the globe of people using your AIs as opposed to Chinese AIs, and your supply-chain security instead. That's what's in the paper at a high level.

items.question: How do you see Beth's techno-capital manifesto in relation to your own account of AI competition in “Natural Selection Favors AIs over Humans”?
items.object: Beth's techno-capital manifesto and Hendrycks's paper “Natural Selection Favors AIs over Humans”

items.question: How do you assess the argument that AI's evolutionary advantage over biological life means we should embrace its replacement of humanity?

items.answer: There's an is-ought distinction. You don't get ought from is. If you're saying that evolution is the case, and technology with AI will be more fit than biological substrate in various competitions, that seems true. That doesn't mean that's a good thing or that we should just let that happen. That doesn't follow. It is certainly a very powerful force that will keep happening and give more and more control to these AI systems and lead to an erosion of control for humanity by default. I don't think we disagree on the description, the is question, as much, but I do think we disagree on the ought, the goodness of those outcomes. items.question: Why do you see airstrikes as unnecessary for states seeking to disrupt AI projects?

items.question: How do you assess the idea of a US Manhattan Project to achieve AI dominance?
items.object: A US Manhattan Project to achieve AI dominance

If you wake up China for this, they would potentially create some sort of Manhattan Project, and I don't know, they might be better at it. They would probably have better information security for it, and they might have a big chunk of the talent. Would it be the majority? I don't know. That's unclear. If we're requiring that they have security clearances, that limits your pool of researchers substantially. If they're researchers, and they're not being paid well, and they're also going in the middle of nowhere, in some place that has a big data center with a big target over it, because it's extremely visible from space and gives off so much heat, it's not like this would be a secret. items.question: Why do you see deployment capacity as an important axis of competition in AI?
items.object: Deployment capacity as an axis of AI competition
items.answer: The competition is not just having the smartest model as well. There's deployment capabilities, not just model-making capabilities. We can see that the AI model providers limit the amount of videos that you can make. This is because of compute limitations in part, and the amount of videos and images. I think with AI agents they'll be running around the clock if they're sufficiently useful. Right now maybe you use your AI systems a few minutes a day, your chatbots, but then you'd be having it run constantly. That's two orders of magnitude more compute required there, and maybe the models are bigger as well. That's a lot, and then more people are wanting it too. You're needing a lot more compute. Your deployment capabilities—how many chips are owned by US hyperscaler companies, Azure, AWS, et cetera—are a very relevant competitiveness variable, because then are they able to serve the customers or not? If China has less than 100,000 GPUs, they can't really serve that many customers. Even if they can make somewhat capable models, that doesn't mean they'll necessarily capture many of the economic benefits that AI may provide, provided there isn't catastrophe. That's a different important axis for competition.

items.question: How do you see the relevance of AI deterrence, competitiveness, and insurance strategies if superintelligence is not technologically feasible soon?

items.answer: We already have AIs helping or influencing AI development in a recursive way: partly automating some code, helping design the chips, helping cool the power plants, helping label some of the data, doing the Constitutional AI-related type of stuff. items.question: How do you assess the room for AI intelligence to keep improving beyond human capabilities before it saturates?
items.object: The potential for AI intelligence to keep improving beyond human capabilities
items.answer: I don't know if it would saturate necessarily. Certainly if they're at some capability level, this might affect the rate of improvement substantially. Obviously there has to be a limit because of physics somewhere, but I would imagine there's a lot of room for improving its ability to handle things of more and more complexity. Some of those sequences, like in those Raven's matrices, you can think of just as ARC-type things. Some have lower Kolmogorov graph complexity; some have higher complexity. That's some notion from theoretical computer science, and I don't think humans are anywhere near the computational limit for that at all. I would guess that number could keep going up. I think fluid intelligence could get really high. The IQ of the AIs, which wouldn't be all the intelligence, would be separate from their long-term memory, visual processing ability, reaction time, et cetera. I think their IQ could get really high, and they could solve extremely difficult mathematics problems and have really good intuitions for puzzles and not take much compute for it. I think that number could keep going up quite a bit. We're quite limited. We've got big brains, but there's not much hardware here. You can imagine a bigger brain that would have pretty substantial capabilities. Human intelligence across generations—there are Flynn effects and things like that, and that has greatly increased. Our brain size is quite limited by what can go through the birth canal. I expect AIs wouldn't have that limit. They could at the very least keep getting faster and faster. You still have Moore's law, and you have GPU improvement rates, which are like 2x every 3 years. You also have scalability and better ability to transfer state than it is with humans, because a lot of this digital computation is more precise than analog. I think they have a variety of substantial advantages. You can better transfer things across generations as well. Nobel Prize winners' descendants are not able to—you know, their descendants kind of go downhill generally. I think they have some pretty substantial advantages that could compound and accumulate. They could do thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and this could provide compounding effects that make them substantially more capable. There may be various points of saturation along the way. It's not like they kept going at that rate; they just copied what was lying around, and then it was harder. You may have getting to human level in some respects, and in some domains it may be harder to keep getting better if you don't have a good measurement or feedback loop. I think it could be quite complicated. I'm agreeing with some points there, but conceptually I still think there's a lot of room to go up in intelligence.

items.question: How do you understand the offense-defense balance across information battles, cybersecurity, and bioweapons?
items.object: The offense-defense balance across information, cybersecurity, and bioweapons
items.answer: I think the offense-defense balance varies a lot by domain. Many information battles might actually be more defense dominant, for instance debates about the world, which would be a reason for things like free speech. Meanwhile, other things might have more of a duality. Really expert-level or competent computer-security teams might experience more of an offense-defense balance, where something is identified and we patch the vulnerability very quickly, so the attackers keep up with the defenders quite well. In other domains, like the software for critical infrastructure, there's more of an offense dominance or attackers' advantage because a lot of the software just doesn't get updated quickly. There are interoperability constraints. The software developer is no longer around. The software was made 30-plus years ago. Nobody even knows that it's there. There aren't strong enough economic incentives for doing this. There are uptime requirements. Software on critical infrastructure for various forms of critical infrastructure is more of a sitting duck, and there you don't experience a good offense-defense balance. Likewise for bioweapons: certainly we have medicine, but we don't have cures for everything. We spend a lot trying to find cures for many sorts of diseases and ways of addressing certain viruses. It's not necessarily the case that there's a new pathogen and we'll just find a cure a day later and it will be mass-proliferated across the globe and everything's taken care of. There is a substantial delay, so it is more offense dominant there too. There are ways you can imagine the attacker having a really substantial advantage, like it propagating throughout society before anybody shows symptoms and lacking various monitoring mechanisms. We're kind of sitting ducks for some of those. It varies by domain. Some parts of cyber have a good offense-defense balance; other parts of cyber don't. Bio seems offense dominant.

items.question: How do you think the offense-defense balance should affect the proliferation of AI capabilities?

items.answer: I think this affects whether you want to propagate the technology. You don't want to give everybody a nuke to make everybody safe. That's not how it works. It's people constraining each other's intent, and some people just won't have their intent be that constrainable. Meanwhile, other things like defenses, home security systems, or fences, you'd want to propagate more. That should affect attitudes for specific types of AI capabilities as well. They're willing to have more far-UV things, more wastewater monitoring, et cetera. That makes things closer to there being more of a balance, or at least not having as much of an attacker's advantage. You may want mass proliferation of these AI capabilities a bit later, once you have some of those safeguards in place.

items.question: How do you understand the risk of losing human control as society becomes increasingly dependent on AI systems?
items.object: Human control as society becomes increasingly dependent on AI systems
items.answer: I describe this at more length in “Natural Selection Favors AI over Humans.” There's a way in which we are becoming more dependent on these AI systems, starting to cede more of our decisions and cognitive processes to them, and there will be more and more pressure to keep doing that without any clear limit at the economic level. A company that has AI systems that are just better than you is going to win because those will be cheaper. At the military level, too, there's a very strong incentive to make the drones more autonomous, because they can be jammed. Signal jamming makes them a lot less effective, so make them autonomously move around. These pressures will keep up such that we'll voluntarily acquiesce a lot of power in society to these sorts of systems. If we do it at a rate where we aren't actually in control, that could be concerning. What does control exactly look like? When is it too much? When is it too irreversible? That's a problem that we have to keep track of. There are different outcomes. One is where you've actually lost control: you can't stop it, reverse it, bargain with it, or substantially steer it, and your fitness as a species is collapsing as a consequence, or your livelihood evaporates. There's a different outcome where you are like a retiree having a big retirement fund, and the AIs are working for you. They are doing your bidding even though you aren't making nearly all of the critical decisions. Those are different outcomes, and it could be insidious or subtle as to whether we actually have some of that counterfactual control versus winding up in an unfortunate situation. At least one thing that can help would be if AIs are better at forecasting or foreseeing outcomes of consequences. If we train them to do that, it could help make us more prescient and avoid some of the outcomes of extreme dependence and an erosion of control. That wouldn't be sufficient, but it would be helpful for seeing farther and knowing what we're getting ourselves into.

These pressures will keep up such that we'll voluntarily acquiesce a lot of power in society to these sorts of systems. If we do it at a rate where we aren't actually in control, that could be concerning. What does control exactly look like? When is it too much? When is it too irreversible? That's a problem that we have to keep track of.

There are different outcomes. One is where you've actually lost control: you can't stop it, reverse it, bargain with it, or substantially steer it, and your fitness as a species is collapsing as a consequence, or your livelihood evaporates. There's a different outcome where you are like a retiree having a big retirement fund, and the AIs are working for you. They are doing your bidding even though you aren't making nearly all of the critical decisions. Those are different outcomes, and it could be insidious or subtle as to whether we actually have some of that counterfactual control versus winding up in an unfortunate situation.

At least one thing that can help would be if AIs are better at forecasting or foreseeing outcomes of consequences. If we train them to do that, it could help make us more prescient and avoid some of the outcomes of extreme dependence and an erosion of control. That wouldn't be sufficient, but it would be helpful for seeing farther and knowing what we're getting ourselves into.
